items.title: Whitney Museum Is Selling a de Kooning Painting Just Three Years After Receiving It
items.summary:
New York’s Whitney Museum is selling a Willem de Kooning painting at Christie’s next week, just three years after it formally received the work as a gift from the family of one of its former presidents.

Yellow River (1958), a large abstract picture dominated by hefty sweeps of blue and yellow, has an estimate of $12 million to $18 million and will appear in Christie’s 20th century evening sale on November 17. The painting is being sold to benefit the museum’s collection, according to Artnet News , which first reported the story and the auction house’s catalog .

Yellow River belonged to David M. Solinger, a lawyer and collector who became the Whitney’s first president from outside the Whitney family in 1966. Solinger bought the painting from Sidney Janis Gallery in 1959, and according to Christie’s, he liked it so much that it hung for a time at the foot of his bed, where he could see it every morning.

Following Solinger’s death in 1996, the painting passed to his wife, Betty Ann Besch Solinger, who promised it to the Whitney in 2011. The work was exhibited at the museum that year, but the gift was not formally completed until 2023, after she passed in 2022. Now, three years later, it is headed back to the market.

This isn’t the first time the Whitney has dabbled with deaccessioning , the practice of selling works from a museum’s permanent collection. In 2023, the museum sent a group of paintings by Edward Hopper, Maurice Prendergast, John Marin, and others to Sotheby’s. It was led by Edward Hopper’s Cobb’s Barns, South Truro (1930–33), which came with an $8 million to…
items.t: Whitney Museum Is Selling a de Kooning Painting Just Three Years After Receiving It

items.title: Former Philadelphia Museum of Art Executive Charged $30K to Company Cards
items.summary:
A former Philadelphia Museum of Art executive admitted on Friday to using company credit cards to make approximately $30,000 in personal purchases, the Inquirer reports .

Latasha Harling, the museum’s former chief people and diversity officer, pleaded guilty to receiving stolen property, averting a trial that had been scheduled for Friday.

Common Pleas Court Judge Leon King II sentenced Harling, 44, to five years of probation for the misdemeanor offense. King also ordered her to pay the museum $30,000 in restitution in monthly installments of at least $500, beginning in January. If she pays the full amount before her probation ends, however, Harling may request early termination of her probation.

Harling joined the museum in November 2023 as its inaugural chief people officer (CPO), overseeing human resources and diversity initiatives. Her budgetary responsibilities, the Inquirer noted, included access to corporate credit cards. An affidavit of probable cause filed in connection with her arrest recounts how museum officials grew suspicious of her activities in January 2025, after being alerted to a series of significant, seemingly personal purchases on her credit card statements. A subsequent audit by the museum’s chief financial officer found that Harling had charged $58,885 in personal expenses to the card since her hiring.

Harling was offered the opportunity to repay $32,565 to the museum, the affidavit states. She resigned shortly thereafter, with the credit card expenses still outstanding. The museum then sought to recover the money: The following February,…
items.t: Former Philadelphia Museum of Art Executive Charged $30K to Company Cards

items.title: Europol Warns of More Aggressive Museum Heists as Thieves Change Tactics and Targets
items.summary:
It seems like news of new museum robberies just keeps coming, particularly in the months following the brazen Louvre heist one year ago. In an attempt to shed light on the phenomenon, Europol published a study in August, Changing Tactics, Changing Targets: The Evolving Nature of Museum Heists , which examines key trends within these more recent crimes, as reported earlier by The Art Newspaper .

What does Europol tell us? For one, the old notion that museum thefts are generally non-violent, or use stealthy tactics such as replacing precious jewels or artworks with convincing fakes, is no longer the case. “Offenders are adopting more direct and confrontational approaches,” as well as “a growing use of force” to break into museums and display cases using tools like sledgehammers, axes, crowbars, and sometimes explosives, states the report. On some occasions, museum workers have been intimidated with weapons, but also directly assaulted. According to the report, Louvre staff and visitors were threatened by the men who broke into the museum during its opening hours on October 19, 2025, and successfully fled with over $102 million worth of the country’s crown jewels.

The kinds of things getting stolen are also changing. In the last few years, thieves have increasingly been going for precious stones and metals such as gold, which can be melted down, cut, or taken apart from their casings and sold without a trace. Plus, these materials attract attention due to a “perception that museum security measures are less robust than those in jewelry stores.”

items.t: Europol Warns of More Aggressive Museum Heists as Thieves Change Tactics and Targets

items.title: Sotheby’s Hedreen Auction Proceeds Will Repay Loan, Not Fund University Museum: Report
items.summary:
A $300 million art donation to Seattle University has been revealed to be more complex than originally reported.

On Monday, Sotheby’s will begin selling approximately 50 works from the collection amassed by Seattle real estate developer and philanthropist Richard “Dick” Hedreen, previously billed as the “largest art gift ever” to a US university. Hedreen said in September that the sale did not mean the promised gift was falling through. Rather, he suggested, the proceeds would help furnish Seattle University’s new art museum, where the collection was eventually expected to hang.

Records newly reported on by The Seattle Times , however, tell a different story: The works are being sold not to fund the museum, but to pay off a debt secured against the collection — a debt Hedreen says stands between him and fulfilling his pledge to the university.

What was originally framed as a donation, in reality, was a pledge: Hedreen, whose firm R.C. Hedreen Co. owns the Grand Hyatt among other Seattle properties, retained the right to buy and sell works from the collection until the gift was finalized. The Sotheby’s auction is expected to generate at least $100 million across a series of sales. As of writing, the overall value of the artwork set for Seattle University is unclear.

The sale spans an expansive sweep of art history. Works by Willem de Kooning, Rashid Johnson, Amy Sherald, and Jonas Wood will be offered alongside Old Masters by Bronzino, Jacopo Pontormo, Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, and Thomas Gainsborough. Leading Sotheby’s offerings is Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on…
items.t: Sotheby’s Hedreen Auction Proceeds Will Repay Loan, Not Fund University Museum: Report

items.title: At NYC’s ADAA Art Fair, Unlimited Shrimp and $2K Diebenkorns
items.summary:
There are many art fairs in New York City, but perhaps none are friendlier than the one hosted by the chummy Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA). 

“We all know each other very well,” Dorsey Waxter, former president of the ADAA and partner at Van Doren Waxter gallery, told Hyperallergic . “We’ve vetted each gallery that comes into the association for levels of excellence and standards. And it’s not so big you can’t have conversations with dealers and find out things about what you’re looking at.”

Jovial conversations about pathbreaking newcomers and long-dead modernists abounded inside the Park Avenue Armory, which provided a needed refuge from the cold nor’easter pummeling Manhattan for Thursday night’s VIP preview.

items.t: At NYC’s ADAA Art Fair, Unlimited Shrimp and $2K Diebenkorns

items.title: 45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds
items.summary:
A new report tracks the challenges facing publications that cover arts and culture. (edit Valentina Di Liscia/ Hyperallergic, image KC Green) Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week. 

The new survey notably identifies a disturbing correlation between censorship concerns, including external pressure from advertisers and sponsors, and financial precarity. The 41% of respondents who said they faced free-speech pressures or threats in the last two years were more likely to report funding declines, throwing into stark relief how what outlets choose to cover — or not — may determine whether they can pay staff and contributors, or keep the lights on altogether.

“Support for Arts and Culture Journalism: A Survey of Independent Publications in the United States” polled 141 independent outlets that cover the arts on issues impacting the field and strategies used to address them. The anonymized respondents are based in 34 states and the District of Columbia, with the highest concentration (38.2%) in the Northeast, and reach an average annual audience of about half a million.
items.t: 45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds

items.title: Manhattan Landlord Sues Kehinde Wiley, Claiming He Owes $36,000 in Unpaid Rent
items.summary:
Artist Kehinde Wiley returned to the New York art scene last week with his first show in the city since he was accused of sexual assault in 2024. Now the famed artist and Obama portraitist faces a legal dispute of a different kind: real estate.

In a complaint filed in New York County Supreme Court, 115 West 11th Street LLC accuses Wiley of failing to pay rent on his apartment in its building since October 1. According to court documents filed November 6, the rent is $18,000 a month, and the landlord is seeking $36,000 in total.

Per the documents, Wiley has lived in the building since September 2023 and signed a lease renewal in July 2025, which was later extended through the end of September. The landlord contends that Wiley did not vacate the apartment when the lease ended and has continued to live there without paying the agreed $18,000 a month.

Wiley has not yet responded to the complaint. A summons, also filed November 6, requires the artist’s attorneys to respond within 20 days.

The complaint was filed on the same day Wiley’s new exhibition, “What the Light Becomes,” opened at Sean Kelly Gallery in New York. The show features a new series of portraits of contemporary New Yorkers. According to the exhibition text, the show is “conceived of as a love letter to New York and a return to the subject of the city that launched Wiley’s career.”

Sean Kelly Gallery did not respond to a request for comment from ARTnews by press time.

Wiley is one of the art world’s brightest stars and one of the few artists who are household names, thanks to his beloved official portrait…
items.t: Manhattan Landlord Sues Kehinde Wiley, Claiming He Owes $36,000 in Unpaid Rent

items.title: The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife
items.summary:
In the summer of 1966, David Hockney began work on one of his most iconic paintings: “ Beverly Hills Housewife ,” a portrait of the arts patron Betty Freeman. She is depicted on her garden patio in front of her sleek, modernist house, which is framed by strips of blue sky and green lawn. A few status symbols surround her — a William Turnbull sculpture, a zebra-skin lounge designed by Le Corbusier, and a mounted antelope head— but the focal point is Freeman in her bright pink dress, gazing wistfully beyond the confines of the canvas.

Critic and novelist James Cahill uses the painting as a jumping off point to expound on the intertwined lives of both artist and muse, as well as to provide a fragmentary snapshot of Los Angeles in the 1960s, in his new book. With The Beverly Hills Housewife: Hockney’s Californian Muse and the World Beyond the Pool (2026), Cahill bounces between formal analysis of the painting, historical anecdotes, and inferences about the broader culture, zigzagging as if driving across LA without a map. Some of the detours prove less relevant to his central narrative than others, but they are nonetheless diverting pit stops on a thoroughly engrossing journey about the friendship between two complex individuals who played formative roles in shaping LA’s cultural landscape.

David Hockney and Betty Freeman at Freeman's home on November 15, 1987 (image courtesy Special Collections & Archives, UC San Diego Library)
items.t: The Secret Life of Hockney's Beverly Hills Housewife

items.title: Tribal Groups Urge Congress to Halt Bill That Threatens Sacred Sites
items.summary:
Tribal organizations are urging legislators to halt the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a bill that would speed up the permitting and review processes of major infrastructure projects and could severely undermine tribal sovereignty over sacred and culturally significant sites. 

The United States Senate advanced the controversial bill for further debate on November 8 amid mounting criticism from Indigenous groups and historic preservation advocates, largely due to the act's narrowing of Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. 

The law mandates federal agencies to weigh the impact of projects on historic properties, oftentimes with required tribal consultation, though BAAJA removes tribal nations from much of the review process. The bill text also curtails several other environmental acts , such as the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act, and pushes for shorter review timelines, the loosening of protections of sacred lands, and less federal oversight.
items.t: Tribal Groups Urge Congress to Halt Bill That Threatens Sacred Sites

items.title: Long-Lost Charles Le Brun Painting Returns to the New Palace in Potsdam
items.summary:
Lost for more than 75 years, a painting by French Baroque artist Charles Le Brun (1619–1690) is now returning to the New Palace in Potsdam’s Sanssouci Park. The news was first reported by the German Press Agency (dpa) following a statement by the Prussian Palaces and Gardens Foundation Berlin-Brandenburg (SPSG).

Court painter to Louis XIV after 1661 and the designer most responsible for the opulent style of the Sun King’s monarchy, Le Brun created the work, a depiction of a sleeping Christ Child with the Holy Family, around 1655. It was acquired in the 1700s by King Frederick the Great (Frederick II) of Prussia for the New Palace, where it hung in one of the guest apartments.

In 1942, to protect it from Allied bombings, much of the art at the Picture Gallery of Sanssouci and the New Palace, including Le Brun’s painting, was evacuated some 60 miles northwest to Schloss Rheinsberg.

On April 29, 1945, the Red Army entered Rheinsberg. Russian troops occupied the building, and a short time later the majority of the paintings housed in the Schloss Rheinsberg were sent to the Soviet Union. However, according to the SPSG , not all of the works arrived there, with some entering private collections in Rheinsberg under “convoluted circumstances.”

Le Brun’s painting was documented as being at Schloss Rheinsberg until July 30, 1945. After that, according to a spokesperson from the foundation, the painting vanished—until it resurfaced at a Berlin auction house in 2021.

The return was made possible by the support of the Ernst von Siemens Art Foundation and the Friends of the…
items.t: Long-Lost Charles Le Brun Painting Returns to the New Palace in Potsdam

items.title: The Alchemical Possibilities of an Artist-Poet Collaboration
items.summary:
In 1982, Puerto Rican artist Papo Colo installed a book-shaped sculpture in the courtyard of El Museo del Barrio in Harlem. Commissioned as part of David Hammons’s Art in the Park program, it unfurled like an accordion across a series of 8-by-4-foot plywood panels co-authored by nearly 40 invited New York artists and poets. Four decades later, seven of those panels form the basis of Octopus and Others , an exhibition that addresses the porous boundary between the word and the image within the more experimental scenes of production from the ‘80s through today.

The first panel in the exhibition is by Colo himself and gestures toward the alchemical, even transcendent possibilities unleashed through the collaboration of artists and poets across distances, languages, and generations. “English Spanish $ Spanglish,” Colo scribbles in white paint against the black-coated plywood. “Vivas poetas individuales X-formed by Colo’s ceremony into collective.” 

Papo Colo, "Look Outside Your World" from the series Photopoems (1979), from the portfolio Photogenics: Photopoems / Acting as Behavior (1983), Duotone prints from the original monoprints (photo Jason Mandella, courtesy El Museo del Barrio)
items.t: The Alchemical Possibilities of an Artist-Poet Collaboration

items.title: The ADAA Fair Is Back, and Sometimes Smaller Really Is Better
items.summary:
Art fairs should do two things: let visitors see art, ideally stuff they haven’t seen before, and help dealers sell that art to people who want to buy it. Simple enough. And yet, somewhere along the way, fairs became so enormous that seeing everything on offer began to feel like an endurance sport.

That’s one reason the newly rechristened Art Dealers Association of America Fair, which opened Thursday night at the Park Avenue Armory, was such a pleasure. With just 63 exhibitors, it’s small enough to navigate without a map, manageable enough to spend time actually looking at the art, and varied enough to reward a little wandering. These may sound like modest achievements, but anyone who’s spent six hours trudging through a convention center will appreciate them.

The setting helps. The Park Avenue Armory still has plenty of its old New York charm, something that’s increasingly hard to come by in an art fair. Organizers have also moved the bar to the center of the exhibition hall, improving the sightlines and making the whole affair feel more open. You can actually see what’s going on across the room, rather than navigating a maze of booths.

Of course, the fair’s return wasn’t entirely straightforward. Last July, the AADA abruptly canceled its 2025 edition, calling the decision a “strategic pause.” The organization subsequently retired the Art Show name and ended its decades-long fundraising partnership with the Henry Street Settlement, which had received more than $38 million through the fair’s benefit previews. The Whitney Museum of American Art is now the beneficiary,…
items.t: The ADAA Fair Is Back, and Sometimes Smaller Really Is Better

items.title: Botanical Artists Show Us What We Stand to Lose
items.summary:
Ascending to the third floor of NYC’s Society of Illustrators this fall is like entering a secret garden. The room is aglow with daylight and rare flora, not in situ, but in the 50 framed winners of its collaboration with the American Society of Botanical Artists’ 29th Annual International Exhibition. The works radiate with majesty, and the intricate sumptuousness is agonizing. Here, the threat of climate change looms. 

With strong sun rays streaming in, the plant-potted upper patio of the Society of Illustrators is a jewel box of windowed light, a parade of watercolors on vellum or watercolor paper bask in the sunlight. Here is awe for Mother Earth and her plants — and these botanical artists — and for the meticulous, enchanting detail and outcry that cherish every bud, stem, leaf, petal, bark, seed, blade, stamen, and root.

Daleen Roodt beside her winning painting "Cinderella's Wonderland" (photo Amy Levine-Kennedy/ Hyperallergic ) (left); Kelsey Wilson, "Red Gems" (2025), watercolor on paper (image courtesy American Society of Botanical Artists) (right)
items.t: Botanical Artists Show Us What We Stand to Lose

items.title: Seven Museums to Host Solo Exhibitions Celebrating Wolf Kahn’s Centennial
items.summary:
Several museums are joining forces to celebrate Wolf Kahn, who rendered his pastoral surroundings in saturated hues and diffused light, on the occasion of the late artist's 100th birthday next October. Unfolding across 2027, Kahn's centennial program is assembled by the artist's namesake foundation, which recently opened a permanent location for its archives in New York City this summer. 

Known for melding the representational with the abstract, Kahn's reputed, lesser-known, and never-before-seen work will be exhibited in locations that shaped his life and career trajectory. Born in 1927 in Germany to a Jewish family, Kahn moved to the United States in 1940 as a refugee during World War II. He got his bearings in New York City, which became an influential home base for the artist throughout his lifetime. 

He also spent a significant amount of time developing his practice in Martha's Vineyard and Provincetown, Massachusetts, where he worked as a studio assistant for Abstract Expressionist Hans Hofmann. He eventually purchased a farm in West Brattleboro, Vermont, where he would spend his summers painting en plein air from 1968 until he died in 2020. Over seven decades, Kahn carved out a reputation for rendering nature through luminous, exaggerated, and arbitrary color, creating a glowing effect across his landscapes.
items.t: Seven Museums to Host Solo Exhibitions Celebrating Wolf Kahn’s Centennial

items.title: Lightsaber Brandished by Darth Vader Auctioned for $4.9 M., Breaking Record for Star Wars Sales
items.summary:
A lightsaber wielded by none other than Darth Vader sold for $4.875 million in a Heritage Auctions sale, breaking the record for Star Wars –related memorabilia.

The treasure was used in Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back (1980) and Star Wars: Return of the Jedi (1983), and also holds the special distinction of having been the weapon central to the former’s famous “I am your father” scene, in which Luke Skywalker learns some surprising news from the figure who had long been his nemesis.

Heritage reported that the sale exceeded that of “Luke Skywalker’s lightsaber and severed hand effects rig” last year (for $3.75 million) and a poster painting for Star Wars: Episode IV—A New Hope in 2025 (for $3.875 million).

About the sale of the lightsaber, one of 27 offered up by Heritage, Brian Chanes, the auction house’s senior director of Hollywood and entertainment, told Los Angeles’s ABC7 Eyewitness News , “I’ve been doing this for 35 years and I’ve never seen a compilation of screen-used lightsabers like this; you know, from the original franchise to the sequels.” He continued: “It’s the one on the set. It’s from the most iconic sequence of the entire franchise. From a memorabilia standpoint this is like the holy grail.”

About sales of the kind in general, Chanes added, “I always tell people that memorabilia, the m-e-m portion is your memories, what you remember when you first saw the first Star Wars film. It basically takes you to the happy place when you first saw it, and it’s a feel-good thing!”
items.t: Lightsaber Brandished by Darth Vader Auctioned for $4.9 M., Breaking Record for Star Wars Sales

items.title: Fake UK Artist Visas Are Being Offered for $132,000, New Investigation Finds
items.summary:
Several companies have been helping migrants apply for UK visas under the government’s Global Talent program by creating fake art portfolios, complete with fake published art criticism and art news, according to a new investigation published by the BBC Friday.

Nigerian art critic Molara Wood told the publication that she had found her name attached to fake online reviews praising the works of two obscure artists, just one instance of the materials created. 

“There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists,” Wood told the BBC . Following the BBC ’s investigation, two Nigerian men’s visas are in the process of being revoked, according to the Home Office. The two claimed to be fine art photographers in their visa applications.

One BBC reporter went undercover to research the companies offering packages through the Global Talent program. The firm said it could supply the reporter with artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation. The reporter had been reassured that the “fully inclusive” would grant them a visa without refusal—the package was priced at more than £100,000 ($132,000). The Home Office told the BBC that the company the reporter had dug out was already under investigation. A spokesperson for the Home Office said that they “will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system” and the “home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused.”

The government’s Global Talent program was…
items.t: Fake UK Artist Visas Are Being Offered for $132,000, New Investigation Finds

items.title: Rhizome Announces Partnership With Electronic Arts Intermix Following Vimeo Censorship Concerns
items.summary:
Earlier this week, Rhizome, the 30-year-old digital art nonprofit that has been affiliated with the New Museum since 2003, announced a pilot program with its internal video hosting platform video.rhizome.org, and Electronic Arts Intermix (EAI). Rhizome hopes to offer VRO, as it’s known, to other digital arts organizations and artists as an alternative to commercial video platforms like Vimeo.

“We think offering artists video hosting is something that could be meaningful for people in the community right now,” Michael Connor, Rhizome’s executive director, told ARTnews . “With the way that the web is going, it’s harder and harder to run a platform the way Vimeo operated a decade ago.”

Rhizome initially set up VRO in 2022, but their plans to offer the technology to others in the digital arts community kicked into high gear this summer following a breakdown in the relationship between Vimeo and EAI, a video and new media distributor with a collection of thousands of digital artworks by over 200 artists.

The trouble started in May, when EAI began receiving emails, which EAI executive director Rebecca Cleman believes were AI-generated, flagging their account for community guideline violations. Karl McCool, EAI’s distribution director, told ARTnews that the two works Vimeo initially flagged were Barbara Hammer’s 1970s films Dyketactics and Women I Love , two of EAI’s most requested films.

EAI wasn’t completely caught off guard by this, McCool explains. He’d heard from colleagues at similarly sized arts organizations, like Collectif Jeune Cinema, a French experimental film…

items.title: Craft in America Concludes its Handwork Series with NORTH and SOUTH
items.summary:
The documentary series Craft in America returns with two new episodes, streaming online now and premiering on PBS this December. These episodes are part of the  Handwork: Celebrating American Craft 2026  initiative, a yearlong project marking the nation’s 250th anniversary and celebrating the diversity of the crafts that define America.

SOUTH and NORTH complete the series’ journey through craft across the United States, which began in December 2025 with episodes EAST and WEST. 

The SOUTH episode explores craft artists who are building an inclusive and hopeful future, such as Jessica Osceola, an artist and member of the Seminole tribe of Florida.

“Making objects is something that we’re just born into,” says Osceola.“Craft links the generations. You’re looking at your past, your present, and your future, and it’s good that the chain never gets broken.”

Along with Jessica and the Osceola-Zepeda family of Naples, Florida, the episode features Ato Ribeiro, an artist in Atlanta, Georgia, who makes wooden quilts inspired by Ghanaian symbols; fiber artist Vicki Essig, who works with silkworms to create art garments in Spruce Pine, North Carolina; stained-glass mosaic artist Sebastian Duncan-Portuondo in Miami Beach, Florida; and Shaka Zulu and Edward Buckner, who participate in the Black Masking Indian society traditions of New Orleans, Louisiana, known for their elaborate beaded costumes.

In NORTH, Craft in America investigates the impact of the northern landscape on artists. Jeremy Frey, a featured artist in NORTH, reflects how his work and the environment are deeply…

items.title: A Toolkit for a Liberated Art World
items.summary:
“Radical politics,” “marginalized communities,” “feminist art” … If you see these terms peppering wall labels at a major museum, there’s an excellent chance the institution behaves in direct opposition to those values and groups. Scholars Amin Husain and Nitasha Dhillon, who were also among the organizers of the historic Strike MoMA protests in 2021, know this pattern all too well. It’s part of the neoliberal capture of art institutions, which Italian curator and activist Marco Baravalle lays bare in his new book, The Battleground of Art . Read on for a review by Husain and Dhillon, who write that it’s a toolkit for building a better, freer art world.

Meanwhile, in the United States, that art world finds itself at a crucial turning point. In the wake of the midterm elections, longtime nonprofit arts leader Jasmine Wahi reminds us that the fight is only beginning. She opines today about the importance of holding Democratic officials accountable not just for redressing the damage inflicted by the Trump administration, but also for taking its responsibility to artists and culture workers seriously. “Rebuilding the same inadequate baseline is not enough,” she explains.

More in the news today, including public backlash against Egypt’s arrest of the editor of an independent publication and San Francisco-based painter Hiroshi Sato’s resistance against Silicon Valley and enshittifcation through his quietly subversive art. Heaven knows we could all use more of that.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

items.title: Hamlet Hail to the Thief could have been rotten but redeems Radiohead’s ‘record that got away’ | Alexis Petridis
items.summary:
The band’s uneven 2003 album has been judiciously reworked to accompany a staging of Shakespeare’s tragedy with quite extraordinary results

According to the programme notes, Thom Yorke had serious reservations about director Christine Jones’ idea to stage a production of Hamlet featuring music from Radiohead’s 2003 album Hail to the Thief. Who can blame him? Many criticisms have been laid at Radiohead’s door but being hopelessly naff isn’t one of them, and, alas, naff is very much the adjective you’d apply to a lot of attempts to meld Shakespeare and rock music.

You’re often in the realm of high camp – portentous, Bard-quoting heavy metal lyrics; Return to the Forbidden Planet’s jokey blending of The Tempest with 50s rock’n’roll; 2015’s These Paper Bullets, which relocated Much Ado About Nothing to swinging London, complete with Beatle-y songs by Green Day’s Billie Joe Armstrong – or of buttock-clenching disasters like Catch My Soul, a 1971 rock adaptation of Othello which required Black American soul singer PP Arnold to star opposite impresario Jack Good, playing the title role in blackface.

items.title: Protesters Urge Steven Spielberg to Boycott MoMA Over Leon Black’s Epstein Ties
items.summary:
Ahead of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) annual benefit for its Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center tonight, November 12, about 20 protesters assembled outside the institution to call on the gala's honoree, Steven Spielberg, to reject the recognition. The protest comes amid growing calls to oust Leon Black from the museum board over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. 

Playwright and theater artist Gracie Gardner was held by security after she entered the museum and chanted in protest of Leon Black. She was subsequently issued a No Trespass Order banning her from MoMA for life and released by security.

Another letter sent to Spielberg by the feminist campaign group We Are UltraViolet, reviewed by Hyperallergic , urges the Academy Award-winning director to boycott MoMA until the institution severs ties with Black and renames the film venue. 

“MoMA has benefited so handsomely from Black that they have named the very room you will be honored in, the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, in his honor,” reads the missive to Spielberg, authored by Elisa Batista, campaign director of UltraViolet. For the past four iterations of the benefit, MoMA has funneled all proceeds into the film center, which was created in 2019 in recognition of a $40 million gift from the private equity tycoon. 

“Mr. Spielberg, you do NOT want your legacy connected to accused abuser and Epstein associate Leon Black,” Batista continues.

Yukiko Yamagata to Helm Print Center New York Print Center New York, home to programs and exhibitions celebrating all the art that's pressed, proofed, and published, announced Yukiko Yamagata as its new executive director this week. 

Her professional profile doesn't immediately scream “print nerd”: Yamagata most recently served as deputy director at Creative Time and previously worked at the Open Society Foundations, where she led a $15.8 million arts and culture fellowship program for socially engaged artists. But one of her earliest roles in the 1990s was as a senior curatorial assistant in the photo department at the Whitney Museum of American Art, and she is a current board member of Women Photograph, an organization focused on equitable practices in photojournalism and visual media.

Yamagata succeeds Judy Hecker , who announced her decision to step down earlier this year after a decade in the role, and is now executive director emerita.

items.title: The Art World's Neoliberal Capture
items.summary:
We first met Marco Baravalle in 2015 at the 56th Venice Biennale, All the World’s Futures , when we were organizing with the Gulf Labor Coalition . The group and our autonomous direct-action wing, Global Ultra Luxury Faction (G.U.L.F.), had been invited by curator Okwui Enwezor to present our research and organizing against migrant worker exploitation in the construction of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi . An artist boycott was underway, direct actions were escalating, and days earlier, on May 1, we had shut down the Guggenheim Museum in New York City.

Through Baravalle, a longtime researcher, curator, and activist, we encountered a network of autonomous spaces in Venice and Milan. These were not simply cultural centers; they formed the infrastructure for collective organizing, resistance, and enacting other worlds.

Eleven years later, The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism (2026) extends this praxis into an important and timely call to action. Drawing on his two decades of experience, Baravalle offers what we have called movement-generated theory and practice , rooted in the dialectic of doing and knowing. The book confronts the neoliberal capture of the art world, while also excavating histories and practices of abolition and autonomy that offer other possibilities.
items.t: How to Free the Art World From Its Neoliberal Capture

items.title: After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins
items.summary:
In the afterglow of the blue-nami , those of us who make, organize, fund, and sustain cultural life are feeling a twinge of hope. But I find myself slipping into a spiral of anxiety as the everyday reality of economic precarity sets back in. Our newly elected Democratic congressional leaders have an opportunity to change that reality — pushing back against Trump is necessary — but it cannot be the full extent of their ambition.

As a curator and the co-director of an arts nonprofit, I’ve been asked what the results mean for the so-called “art world.” My first response was cynical: “not much.” At least not immediately. An election does not directly restore a canceled grant or pay an artist’s rent. And even a return to the funding landscape that existed before Trump took office in 2025 would leave us with a system that was already failing the people expected to sustain it.

Instead, the midterm election results should serve as an opening to hold Democrats in Congress accountable for making arts and cultural life materially sustainable, not simply to defend an inadequate system from further attack. That mandate concerns whose histories are told, who gets paid to make art, and who gets to define the country’s future. It also concerns whether the people doing that work can afford to keep going.
items.t: After the Midterms, the Real Work for Arts and Culture Begins

items.title: Human Rights Orgs Denounce Egypt's Arrest of Mada Masr Editor Lina Attalah
items.summary:
Prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, co-founder and editor-in-chief of Egypt's independent news outlet Mada Masr , is facing a one-year prison sentence among other penalties in a targeted crackdown on press freedom. 

Summoned to court in Cairo last month on charges of publishing false news and operating the news site without a license, Attalah learned during the proceedings that she had been handed a year-long sentence in absentia on similar charges in 2024 without her knowledge. 

Human rights and press freedom organizations, including Reporters Without Borders , Human Rights Watch , and the International Federation for Human Rights , have publicly condemned the charges against the journalist and Mada Masr , decrying her prosecution as a “Kafkaesque miscarriage of justice.”

items.title: Caryl Churchill’s magnificent Cloud 9 reaches for the skies – the National Theatre has done it proud
items.summary:
National Theatre, London
The experimental 1979 drama gleefully muddles roles in a century-spanning caper that bounces from colonial Africa to hippy London

Caryl Churchill’s time-hopping 1979 drama is not revived as often as it might be, perhaps because it is so magnificently madcap. Bouncing from a first act satirising Victorian life in colonial Africa to a second act exploring sexual liberation in 1970s London, it could easily roll off-kilter in the wrong hands. There is also its complicated framework. Cloud 9 is a play in two distinct parts which follows some of the characters a century on, although they only age 25 years in that time and are played by different actors through ironic cross-casting.

Thankfully this crisp, handsome and note-perfect revival lands in exactly the right hands with director Dominic Cooke, clear as crystal despite the complications, sizzling with satire but showing itself to be a deadly serious, and still highly topical, play about identity beneath its playful sending up of everything from empire and Britishness to the confinements of marriage.

items.t: Caryl Churchill’s magnificent Cloud 9 reaches for the skies – the National Theatre has done it proud

items.title: ‘Thicky thicky dumb dumb’ satirist Cody Dahler on his viral videos: ‘my material is presented to me on a silver platter!’
items.summary:
The writer and podcaster on why politics is made to seem more complicated than it is and his mission to unpack world events for everyone

Why did you get into comedy?
My mum was a professional dancer and always encouraged me to perform. Given that I have zero rhythm, comedy was my other option. She wrote me a poem called Mrs Brown’s Moggy, about a cat that was often very soggy, for my school’s talent show. Because you can’t tell the difference between real and polite laughter at the age of six, I assumed I’d killed my first gig and convinced myself I was born to do nothing else.

Where do you find your material?
In a world where Robert Jenrick claims Nigel Farage has “probably done more than almost anybody to stand against racism”, the answer is that my material is presented to me on a silver platter each morning.
